title: AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk
pitch: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents.
about_excerpt: Source-grounded AI governance intelligence for humans and agents. Like Comment Story Updates AI Governance Watch turns source-backed AI governance research into a shared briefing workspace for people and browser agents. Inspiration AI governance information is scattered across legislation, agency announcements, standards, procurement records, civil-rights proceedings, and technical guidance. Government leaders and policy professionals often need a concise briefing, but the distinctions behind that briefing matter. A proposal is not an enacted law. A publication date may differ from the underlying event date. An official announcement is not proof of an outcome. A general AI summary can easily blur those boundaries. We built AI Governance Watch to explore a more trustworthy model. The website remains the authority for its research and actions, while a browser agent helps the user search, verify, compare, and organize the information. What it does AI Governance Watch is a public, standalone WebMCP Briefing Desk built around a dated governance snapshot and a 62-entry Source Ledger. The application exposes four focused WebMCP tools: search_updates searches the locally bundled governance report using text and structured filters. get_source_record retrieves an exact Source Ledger entry by its registered identifier. compare_updates compares developments while preserving their dates, jurisdictions, statuses, confidence labels, and sources. build_briefing assembles selected records into a visible, session-only briefing for human review. A user can ask a browser agent to find developments relevant to a government leader, verify the underlying sources, compare the most important records, and construct a briefing focused on implementation, procurement, or public accountability. The resulting briefing appears directly in the application. The human can review, reorder, remove, or clear its contents before relying on it. This is a strong use case for WebMCP because traditional browser agents must interpret layouts, cards, filters, and buttons to determine what an application can do. That approach can be fragile when a page contains legally or operationally significant distinctions. WebMCP allows AI Governance Watch to expose its real domain functions as structured tools. The agent receives validated parameters, stable record identifiers, bounded outputs, and explicit fields for status, confidence, jurisdiction, event date, publication date, and source. How we built it The project uses the WebMCP Imperative API through document.modelContext.registerTool . The four tools register only on the public /webmcp route. No tools register on the application’s unlock page or protected monitor routes. Each tool has a strict JSON Schema and repeats validation at runtime. Every registration promise is awaited before the interface reports that the tools are available. An AbortController manages the registration lifecycle and removes the registrations when the React component unmounts, preventing duplicate tools during remounts. The three research tools are read-only. The briefing tool changes only visible session-level React state. It does not write to a database, publish content, send messages, download files, or contact an external service. All tool results are returned as valid, bounded JSON strings. A single JSON.parse() exposes the top-level ok field and the applicable results, source record, comparison items, or briefing details. The implementation uses the application’s locally bundled August 22, 2026 report and Source Ledger without adding a crawler, external AI provider, or autonomous publishing system. AI Governance Watch treats source-derived material as untrusted content and labels every WebMCP tool accordingly. The implementation includes strict validation, same-origin exposure, read-only annotations, bounded outputs, exact identifiers, visible and reversible state, registration cleanup, and no database or network writes. The standalone route includes dated-snapshot and independence disclosures. It is not affiliated with, endorsed by, sponsored by, or published by the Maryland Responsible AI Council, the State of Maryland, or any government body. If WebMCP is unavailable, the human interface continues to function and explains how to use a supported browser. Existing project disclosure The base Maryland AI Governance Monitor was created on August 22, 2026. Verified pre-challenge baseline commit: c5543d31d7cfc9bd4492bc539112c8801bada8b9 The WebMCP tools, standalone Briefing Desk, shared human-agent state, validation, tests, documentation, and public challenge interface were added during the WebMCP Challenge submission period. Final deployed challenge implementation: 310114de0dfcc426b19f9f2b438b9e7c54dbd487 Public standalone repository commit: 95b584f512cf27ca1ef9a3244f0121626f7a1799 Only the WebMCP extension and human-agent briefing workflow added during the challenge period are presented as challenge work. Challenges we ran into The main challenge was enabling useful agent action without weakening the information boundaries that make a governance monitor trustworthy. Search results needed to remain compact while preserving their status, confidence, source, jurisdiction, and two distinct date fields. The state-changing tool also needed to create meaningful collaboration without producing a hidden or irreversible external side effect. We also needed to separate the challenge project from the broader credential-protected Maryland monitor. The final /webmcp route is publicly accessible and uses a dedicated AI Governance Watch shell, while every existing monitor route remains protected. The resulting design keeps the agent workflow deterministic, inspectable, reversible, and under human control. Accomplishments that we're proud of Converted a human-first research interface into a genuine agent surface. Exposed a complete research-to-briefing workflow through four focused tools. Preserved exact sources, dates, statuses, and confidence labels. Created shared application state between the browser agent and human reviewer. Made the challenge desk publicly accessible without exposing the protected monitor. Demonstrated practical human-agent collaboration beyond a technical proof of concept. Added security annotations, runtime validation, output limits, failure handling, and lifecycle cleanup. Required no new backend, database, crawler, or external AI service. Published a clean standalone repository with no credentials, runtime secrets, authentication implementation, or unrelated application code. Verified all four tools in the live production application using Google Chrome 152 with WebMCP testing enabled. Confirmed that build_briefing creates visible state that a human can reorder, remove, clear, and reset on reload. Documented the exact pre-challenge baseline and challenge-period extension. What we learned WebMCP is most valuable when it exposes an application’s real domain capabilities instead of turning every button into a tool. Four carefully designed functions were enough to let an agent complete a meaningful governance research workflow while keeping the website responsible for its evidence, validation, and state. We also learned that human-agent collaboration does not require unlimited autonomy. A narrow, visible, and reversible action can provide significant value while preserving trust. The project demonstrated that a website can remain the authority for its data and actions while giving agents a structured, safer way to assist the person using it. What's next for AI Governance Watch: A Source-Grounded WebMCP Briefing Desk Future versions could add versioned governance snapshots, user-approved exports, role-specific briefing formats, change detection between reports, claim-level evidence tracing, and additional vetted records. A private editorial pipeline could monitor an approved source registry, identify candidate developments, and route them for human verification before they enter a published snapshot. Any live ingestion, persistent storage, customer-specific workspace, or external action would require separate security, privacy, and editorial review.
